title: Solo game dev business - does it even make sense to develop small games anymore since anyone can build and clone them in minutes with AI?
author: ImpressiveFocus303
selftext:
In the means of solo game dev business - does it even make sense to develop small games anymore since anyone can build and clone them in minutes with AI?

I know that game development business is a bad business, as more than 95% of released games don't make any money. But if I have to insist, I wonder, does it even make sense to try develop and sell small games, such as incremental idles? I've built few incremental idle games in less than 10 prompts with Fable. Everything works and the only thing that needs to be done is fine tuning and reskinning the games, so it doesn't look like they were made by AI. 

Unless a game is complex, I wonder, how (solo) game developers will create games with a competitive advantage (the moat) so the games can't be immediately cloned?

  
what's your take on this?

comments.author: Neon_Camouflage
comments.body:
>I wonder, how (solo) game developers will create games with a competitive advantage

The same way they did before AI. By having a good idea and spending more than a day building it with the tools at hand.

replies.author: Technical_Ideal9
replies.body: This is it, it's really all about a good idea and marketing, nothing else matters.

comments.author: YKLKTMA
comments.body:
I have bad news for the vast majority of people here.

You probably shouldn't make something that can be built in a handful of prompts. It's just a waste of time and tokens. AI slop ends up in the same massive pile at the bottom of Steam as amateur projects, asset flips, and other AI slop made in a few prompts. All of those games make pennies.

Actually making a game has never really been the hardest part. Making a game that people actually want to buy has not become any easier because of AI tools, and it never will. Concord is a perfect example of how even with effectively unlimited resources, you can still make a game that nobody wants even for free.

To make a good game, you need to understand very clearly who you are making it for and why those people should want to pay for it.

Game development is an iterative process. You need to build prototypes and playtest them with your target audience, collect and analyze feedback, and only if the prototype shows promise does it make sense to actually build the full game. And throughout development, you need to keep playtesting regularly in order to polish the game for its target audience.

comments.author: thenameofapet
comments.body: Even if this were true, game dev is an iterative process. Building a working prototype is the first step. You then need to play test it and make changes based on feedback as the project grows.

comments.author: Total-Box-5169
comments.body: There are lots of low effort clones that are not fun to play. Fine tuning the game to make every interaction and every detail satisfactory takes forever.

comments.author: apisol
comments.body: You can't one shot multi-system games currently - LLMs output is based on what is trained as acceptable enough to not result in negative reinforcement, you need to do a lot more prompting than simply "make me an FPS with balh blah blah" to have something anywhere near a handmade game. Media content needs human oversight if you are trying to avoid generic AI slop.
